newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iraq seen continuing sanctions evasion.
newsitem.headline: Iraq seen continuing sanctions evasion.

text.p: Iraqi efforts to smuggle goods through Gulf waters have not subsided in recent months and a U.S.-led multinational patrol enforcing U.N. sanctions has intercepted many vessels, a U.S. official said on Thursday.
"We have seen, in terms of traffic, about the same level over the last several months," said Commander T. McCreary, a spokesman for the Multinational Interception Force (MIF).
"Iraq has been continually attempting to evade sanctions but because of the effectivenes of the force a lot has been stopped. This has not stopped attempts," he added.
McCreary said patrols had intercepted three or four vessels per month and contraband worth $3 million since August.
He said that some ships carrying food or medicine to Iraq, which are not covered by the sanctions, also tried to smuggle in heavy parts for trucks and cars, and computer equipment.

The multinational force has been checking shipping in the Gulf to enforce a U.N. trade embargo imposed on Iraq after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait. Iraq had complained to the United Nations that the patrols had violated its territorial waters.
Iraq was still smuggling out diesel fuel, gas oil and dates, he said.
The United States circulated dozens of documents to a U.N. sanctions committee on Tuesday to prove contraband Iraqi oil was being transported through Iranian waters in violation of the sanctions.

U.S. deputy representative to the United Nations Edward Gnehm, in a note to the committee enclosing the documents, said they related to vessels intercepted and diverted by ships of the MIF, operating under the authority of a 1990 Security Council resolution.

Gnehm said the documents "demonstrate that each vessel loaded Iraqi petroleum products in an Iraqi port and either used Iranian territorial waters or presented forged/falsified Iranian documents in attempting to avoid diversion by the MIF."
Iran has repeatedly denied U.S. claims it was cooperating with Iraq to violate U.N. sanctions.
McCreary said some vessels had used Iranian waters to evade the sanctions.
"Vessels have attempted to use Iranian waters to evade interception, some get caught in different locations. Several trying to use Iranian waters have been boarded," he said.

Since 1994, the patrols have diverted about 90 vessels carrying contraband cargo. Ships found to be violating the sanctions are normally turned over to Gulf Arab states for inspection. Contraband oil or goods are sold and the proceeds deposited in a U.N. escrow account.
